entities.name: Andrzej Hieronim Zamoyski
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Count Andrzej Hieronim Franciszek Zamoyski (died February 10, 1792) was an influential Polish magnate, statesman, and legal reformer during the tumultuous final decades of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth. A scion of the powerful Zamoyski family, he served as the Grand Crown Chancellor from 1764 to 1767, becoming a key architect of King Stanisław August Poniatowski's early reform initiatives. His efforts were set against a backdrop of accelerating political decay, foreign interference, and the looming threat of the Partitions, making his commitment to the Commonwealth's regeneration both vital and ultimately tragic.

Zamoyski's most enduring contribution was his leadership in drafting the "Zamoyski Code" (Kodeks Zamoyskiego), a comprehensive legal codification commissioned by the Sejm in 1776. This ambitious project aimed to streamline and modernize the Commonwealth's antiquated legal system, proposing radical reforms such as limiting the power of the liberum veto, strengthening the executive, and extending certain rights to the burgher class while restricting the absolute power of the magnates over their serfs. Though the Code was ultimately rejected by the Sejm in 1780 due to opposition from conservative elements and pressure from foreign powers—particularly Russia, which saw a stronger Poland as a threat—it represented a profound intellectual and political effort to save the state through internal reform.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Andrzej Hieronim Zamoyski's Zamoyski Code represented a profound, albeit ultimately unsuccessful, attempt to prevent the collapse of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth through comprehensive legal and political reforms, directly influencing subsequent efforts like the Constitution of May 3, 1791.
